posts.title: Costco wants a bigger slice of the online-sales pie
posts.author: amowreader32
posts.excerpt: Shopping at Costco has never been designed for convenience. posts.content:
Shopping at Costco has never been designed for convenience. Costco members love the brand for its giant warehouses, supersized products and low prices, but they know they’ll have to trudge through the supersized store and often wait in long lines to snag their beloved Kirkland Signature items or $1.50 hot dog and soda combo.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, however, more shoppers are turning to delivery for household goods and groceries. Big box companies like Target and Walmart have seen investments in online shopping and delivery infrastructure pay off as ecommerce sales drive growth.

Costco has finally stepped up delivery options to compete after years of limited delivery for select online-only products. In September, Costco announced it was bringing DoorDash delivery options to its U.S. warehouses and expanding Uber Eats delivery options, allowing members to skip the line and get same-day delivery of products from groceries to tech to clothing and beyond.

Inflation and the rising costs of goods have made shoppers more likely to hunt for a bargain online. So far this year, gas and grocery expenses account for about 13.5% of individuals’ income, according to an analysis from Bank of America. The result is shoppers are “trading down” or shopping for cheaper products instead of splurging on higher-value items.

But experts and investors wonder whether Costco can continue to entice members to shop and spend big when choosing delivery.

“You have to walk the aisle, you have to try the sample, you buy it,” said Stanley Lim, associate professor of supply chain management at Michigan State University. “It’s this atmosphere that entices customers to come to the stores.”

Go inside and spend big

Costco’s warehouse-style shopping experience is designed to push shoppers to splurge—offering cheap churros or gasoline to draw customers in while showcasing product samples and advertising big ticket items on the floor. These pricier products, along with membership fees, help balance Costco’s budget.

Across big-box retailers, Costco is known as the low price leader, selling bulk products at or near wholesale price.

“Costco is the first one to lower prices and the last ones to raise them,” said Brett Husslein, an analyst for Morningstar Research.

Costco’s membership is key to its low prices. Shoppers pay a $65 annual fee for the basic tier or $130 a year for the executive membership that boasts perks such as early shopping access and cash back on purchase. To order Costco products online or through third-party delivery apps, shoppers must hold a Costco membership. Membership fees bring in 2% of the company’s total revenue, or about $6 billion annually.

In return, Costco purposefully sells many items below cost to drive customer traffic, like whole rotisserie chickens or Kirkland Signature gasoline.

Costco’s also betting you’ll be swayed by a Traeger smoker, inflatable bouncehouse or pack of Disneyland tickets before you make it to checkout. These purchases bloat the average spend, or ticket, a shopper makes.

“There are impulse buys,” Husslein said. “When you’re at Costco, it's a bit of a treasure hunt in there.”

Camryn Gordon, a 28-year-old living in Los Angeles, considers herself a lifelong Costco member and a firm believer that the warehouse’s shelves will speak to her in lieu of a grocery list.

“Part of the Costco experience is you never know what you’re going to buy or what Costco is going to tell you to buy,” Gordon said. “The longer I spend in there, the more money I do end up spending.”

But it’s difficult to replicate this type of impulse shopping in a digital shopping experience, Lim said. “I don’t think you can offer the same treasure hunt experience online.”

The need for a delivery network

Costco has offered delivery for products not sold in stores for decades; the company first tested delivery for specialty high-end products in 1992 and launched costco.com in 1998, according to earning reports published those years. Today, Costco delivery takes at least two days and is free for orders over $75, a poor offering compared to same-day delivery options provided by competitors.

“Costco is like the worst company that offers delivery service,” said Cristina Morales, analyst at Punto Casa de Bolsa SA de CV. “Amazon or even Walmart has a very superior online platform and have much more efficient delivery services than Costco.”

Consumers’ appetite for grocery pickup and delivery options has grown dramatically since the pandemic. A recent poll from Gallup found 15% of Americans order groceries online for pickup or delivery weekly, up from 4% in 2019.

Part of the trend is driven by shoppers’ desires for convenience, particularly among young people. During Costco’s latest earnings call, Costco CEO Ron Vachris noted that members who use delivery are, on average, younger and looking for more immediacy of delivery.

“They are still visiting the clubs regularly, but they use these [deliveries] as fill-in shops and some may use them even more frequently than that,” Vachris said.

Costco, unlike Amazon or Walmart, relies exclusively on third-party logistics providers, which means service quality can fall below these competitors who own end-to-end fulfillment networks. But if Costco were to own its own delivery network, MSU’s Lim said, it would be costly to move bulky items and could cannibalize the in-store treasure hunt experience that drives the bulk of profits.

Costco did not respond to emailed questions from the Times Square Investment Journal.

In 2025, digitally-enabled sales made up 10% of Costco’s total sales, according to the company’s annual report, while Target and Walmart logged 20% of merchandise sales originated online. Over the past year, Costco’s online sales have grown, rising 19.5% year over year and made up 19% of comparable sales, according to its latest reported quarter.

Recently, Costco’s seen digitally-enabled sales drive membership renewal rates and higher levels of customer spending, Husslein said.

From warehouse to doorstep

As of September, Costco members in the U.S. can order delivery items using DoorDash or UberEats. In October, DoorDash announced it would acquire InstaCart, which may also expand Costco’s delivery options on InstaCart in the future.

Costco shares have risen 25% year-to-date, as of close Nov. 10. Since the deal, Costco’s released its fiscal year 2026 results ended August 30, reporting 10% year-over-year growth in revenue at $297.2 billion and 14% annual increase in profits, at $9.2 billion. The company’s share price grew by a fifth after its release. Analysts expect Costco’s revenues to hit $326.6 billion in fiscal year 2027.

“The idea of using or partnering with a third-party platform is to target a slightly different segment of customers … who are doing a ‘top off run’ in the middle of the week,” Lim said. These customers are more likely to pay a premium on products like when they run out of coffee or need a special ingredient for that night’s dinner.

The partnership also exposes Costco products and memberships to a non-Costco audience by having them visible on UberEats’ or DoorDash’s app. While shoppers can browse Costco products in-app, they must confirm their membership in the app or create a Costco membership online before placing an order.

A third-party delivery service may be more convenient, but shoppers pay a markup of 10% to 30%, Lim said, in addition to a delivery charge for products sold on DoorDash and UberEats.

For some Costco members, that added charge is worth avoiding Costco’s warehouses entirely. Many Costco warehouses experience overcrowding due to heavy foot traffic, Husslein said, a pain point Costco is looking to relieve by opening additional warehouses.

Gordon, the 28-year-old in LA, says she avoids shopping at her local Costco any time after 11 a.m. due to crowding.

As Costco adds more third-party apps for shoppers to use, it also increases the number of contractors fulfilling orders in the store and possibly adding to congestion or emptying shelves, Lim noted. Leaning too far into third-party delivery can make it harder for Costco to maintain its reputation in areas of operations over which Costco doesn’t have direct control, Lim said.

While Costco’s treasure hunt may no longer be a necessary part of the shopping experience for members, it still remains a pull for shoppers like Gordon. Gordon said she’s ordered Costco items via delivery service in the past for must-have items, like cat food, but she doesn’t plan to make a habit of it.

“I like that they offer it,” Gordon said. “And if more people use it, that's fine. Maybe there'll be less people in Costco. But I am definitely an in-person shopper.”

posts.title: Run It Back: How Nike Is Putting Athletes First Again
posts.author: simongalkevich-2-2-2
posts.excerpt: Down 20 points in the fourth quarter against No.1 Ohio State, the Texas Longhorns looked out of answers. posts.content:
Down 20 points in the fourth quarter against No.1 Ohio State, the Texas Longhorns looked out of answers. What more than 100,000 fans packed into Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium witnessed next was a stunner for college football.

The home team executed three consecutive 12-plus-play drives, capped by Hollywood Smothers leaping over a wall of defenders with just 25 seconds left, to pull off a 24-23 victory.

Feeling the stadium shake firsthand on that sweltering September night was Daniel-Yaw Miller, founder of SportsVerse, a newsletter covering the intersection of sports and culture.

“It was without a doubt the most electrifying live sports moment I've experienced since moving to the States a couple of years ago,” says the Englishman.

When the final whistle blew, the Longhorns’ unthinkable late-game charge may not have been the only comeback sealed that night.

UT CAMPUS TAKEOVER

In the week leading up to the biggest game of the early college football season, the University of Texas campus belonged to a sportswear giant in the middle of a major turnaround.

Nike continues to navigate a years-long slump that has wiped out over $200 billion in market value since late 2021. Its root cause lay in an identity shift: under former CEO John Donahoe, Nike was leaning too heavily on legacy lifestyle franchises like the Dunk and Air Force 1. Elliott Hill, who took over in October 2024, is trying to bring the brand back to its athletic roots.

“Sport Offense” is Elliott Hill's push to realign the company around athletes, individual sports and performance innovation. The initiative sits at the heart of Hill’s broader “Win Now” turnaround strategy, whose objectives also include clearing excess inventory and repairing wholesale retail relationships.

Pulling back from traditional retail partners such as Foot Locker and Dick’s was another reason for Nike losing market share to rivals like On and Hoka. Between 2016 and 2025, Nike's share of the US sports footwear market dropped from 40 to 30%, according to Euromonitor.

“Sports is where Nike has a big advantage, because they have the most sponsorships, athletes, leagues,” says David Swartz, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar. “So the ‘Sport Offense’ strategy makes all the sense.“

That week in September, Nike invited UT students to a morning run along Lady Bird Lake with Nike Running that also included free breakfast and t-shirt giveaways; a night workout at the Longhorns’ football weight room with Nike Training and a yoga session with NikeSKIMS, which also offered students discounts at its pop-up store.

UT legend Kevin Durant returned to Austin to welcome four new members to Team KD, his Nike partnership that sponsors and mentors Texas basketball student-athletes. Meanwhile, 13 more Longhorns across eight sports joined the Blue Ribbon Elite program, where Nike partners with universities to sign whole cohorts of elite athletes as brand representatives. Its roster now features five Texas football players, including Ryan Wingo, whose touchdown ignited a historic fourth-quarter comeback (notably missing is Arch Manning, a brand ambassador for Nike competitor Vuori).

“This was Nike surrounding a moment, deploying our full ‘Sport Offense,’” Nike Chief Executive Officer Elliott Hill said in October on the company’s fiscal first-quarter  earnings call with analysts. “Something no one else can do. It was the kind of focus on the ground game that helps us become more locally relevant.”

BETTING ON ATHLETES

Having spent the week in Austin, Miller sees the UT campus programming as the blueprint for Nike’s future.

“This is how Nike is trying to win back young consumers, a demographic where they used to be a no-brainer choice, but aren't anymore,” he says. “These activations are designed to drive ‘brand heat’ and customer loyalty.”

At the same time, the Blue Ribbon Elite program — rapidly expanding since its December launch and now including over 100 collegiate stars nationwide — serves as the latest reminder that athlete endorsements remain the cornerstone of Nike’s identity.

The company’s more-than-40-year partnership with basketball legend Michael Jordan stands out as a textbook example of a successful athlete deal. In fiscal 2026, Jordan Brand shoes and apparel generated $7 billion in sales, or roughly 15% of Nike’s $46.4 billion total revenue.

Through Blue Ribbon Elite Nike recruited Louisiana State University basketball star MiLaysia Fulwiley and football standouts Colin Simmons (UT) and Jordan Seaton (LSU). The company, in turn, is positioning itself for future professional partnerships, notes Katherine Rowe, founder of advisory firm The Playbook and a UT alumna, while at the same time “giving students and fans more reasons to engage with the brand today.”

“The ‘Sport Offense’ is driving results. As Elliott Hill previously said, we have learned through the ‘Sport Offense’ that focus wins. When teams get closer to the athlete, the consumer and the marketplace, they make better decisions,” Nike said to The Times Square Investment Journal in an emailed statement.

Currently, Nike’s massive roster of elite athletes features LeBron James and Durant in basketball; Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland in soccer; Rory McIlroy in golf and Aryna Sabalenka in tennis.

The lineup suffered a setback in September, when French soccer superstar Kylian Mbappé opted not to extend his contract with Nike and left for On. Given that Ronaldo, James and Durant are all retiring soon, does Mbappé’s exit spell trouble for Nike?

Sydney Goodman, analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, doesn’t think so. “All three hold lifetime deals with Nike, so their signature shoes will continue to be sold,” she says. “Nike also has tons of younger athletes, including Caitlin Clark and many men's basketball players.”

A standout guard for the Women’s National Basketball Association’s Indiana Fever, Clark has become the face of Nike’s bet on women's sports. Her Caitlin 1 signature shoe nearly sold out less than two hours after its release in October. The W’s next superstar, JuJu Watkins from University of Southern California, earlier this year became the first athlete to co-create a design for the Nike LeBron shoes series.

Beyond names, Nike also has teams. Lots of them.

On that historic September night in Austin, both Texas and Ohio State wore the Nike Swoosh logo, a sight that is hardly unique. With the addition of the University of Miami, Nike now equips 48 of the 68 elite college sports programs, notes Rowe.

That dominance extends to major American pro leagues, where Nike exclusively provides apparel for the National Football League (through 2038), the National Basketball Association (2037) and Major League Baseball (2029).

INNOVATING THE PRODUCT

Sponsorship contracts are an important part of the Sport Offense strategy, but securing leagues and athletes may not be enough for Hill, now in his third year at the helm, to win back Wall Street’s enthusiasm.

Following weaker-than-expected earnings and a disappointing outlook for the year, Nike’s stock plunged below $32 for the first time since September 2013. The shares have since rebounded, closing at $38 on Nov. 13. Still, down 41% for the year, the stock is hovering near its worst year on record.

Focus on performance innovation is another pillar of Sport Offense. Hill merged the design, product and innovation teams across all Nike’s brands into a single athletes-focused department.

Nike’s running division delivered the first measurable results from this shift, posting double-digit growth and sixth consecutive quarter of gains even as overall revenue fell 5% to $45.9 billion. The sportswear giant’s leadership attributed the progress to strong sales of the Vomero shoe line, which is endorsed by legendary runners like Faith Kipyegon and Sha'Carri Richardson and emphasizes extra cushioning for runners’ feet.

“The combination of ZoomX and ReactX foams makes Vomero 18 feel really enjoyable on long runs,” says running coach Amanda Brooks. “The softness doesn’t leave, but you never feel like the shoe is sucking away your energy.”

Nike drops its next running shoe for marathoners in January. But the Apex model is already making headlines. On Nov. 1, Swede Andreas Almgren won the New York City Marathon, wearing a pair of Apex.

This category rebound, however, closely mirrors broader US footwear sales as running outpaced all other sports categories in the first half of the year, growing 13% in both dollars and units, according to data provider Circana.

And the latest results of Nike’s competitors tell a similar story: running-focused brands On and Hoka reported 17% and 8% sales growth respectively in their latest quarters, while brands like Lululemon, Under Armour and Puma have all been in the red alongside Nike’s overall business.

“Overall, Nike is still losing share and underperforming the market,” says Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData. “This is a consequence of the company’s stumbles, but it also reflects the fact that Nike is still the market leader, which makes it a natural target for all the brands that are expanding.”

Swartz identifies On as a particular threat for Nike. “Today, On is still more than 90% footwear,” he says. “But their apparel business is growing. They’re already having success in tennis. They’re launching football with the help of Thierry Henry and Kylian Mbappé. So there will be more competition for Nike.”

Analysts estimate Nike revenue will decrease to $42.9 billion in the fiscal year ending May 2027, down nearly 8% from the prior year. Morningstar's Swartz expects the company to make $1.7 billion in profit, a 45% annual drop.

For Hill, growth in running might be the first touchdown but completing a turnaround will require more time and progress. The executive sees that September game in Austin as the prototype for the company.

“What stood out to me about Texas' comeback win was how they got there,” Hill said on the call with analysts in October. “A series of methodical drives, a few calculated risks, extra effort in critical moments. They stayed committed to the plan and eventually the scoreboard caught up.”

Analysts remain skeptical.

On a scale from 1 to 5, in which 5 is a buy and a 1 is a sell, Nike’s stock now has a consensus analyst recommendation of 3, its lowest on record, according to Bloomberg.

posts.title: Yum! Brands earnings dragged by cyclospora outbreak hitting Taco Bell
posts.author: irene-adeline-milanez
posts.excerpt: A foodborne illness outbreak linked to lettuce served at Taco Bell clouded Yum! Brands third quarter. Yum, which owns Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill, reported an adjusted earnings per share of $1.56, exceeding Wall Street's estimate of $1.51. The adjusted EPS excludes the gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut. Revenue increased…
posts.content:
A foodborne illness outbreak linked to lettuce served at Taco Bell clouded Yum! Brands third quarter.

Yum, which owns Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill, reported an adjusted earnings per share of $1.56, exceeding Wall Street's estimate of $1.51. The adjusted EPS excludes the gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut. Revenue increased 4% year-over-year to $2.05 billion, but fell slightly short of analyst forecasts.

Yum! Brands contended with the cyclospora outbreak at Taco Bell as broader inflationary pressures continued to challenge the restaurant industry. The company continues to be reliant on Taco Bell's recovery and KFC's international expansion, while cautious consumer spending weighs on fast-food demand.

“It's a tough macroeconomic environment for a number of reasons. Yum! Brands' customers tend to skew toward lower-income consumers,” said John Gordon, Pacific Management Consulting Group analyst. “Those customers are proportionately going to be in more difficult shape.” Consumer prices rose 3.7% from prior year.

The most important measure of Yum's underlying performance was same-store sales, which track sales at restaurants. Worldwide same-store sales were flat compared with the previous year, excluding Pizza Hut. Taco Bell's same-store sales fell 4%, while KFC's increased 1%.

Taco Bell's decline was largely tied to a summer Cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce served at some of its U.S. restaurants. The disruption hurt customer traffic, but the company said sales improved as the quarter progressed. “With their reputation and their strength, they can recover from this,” Gordon said.

Promotions, including $1 Taco Tuesdays for loyalty members, and other value offers have helped attract customers and increased membership sign-ups. Offering inexpensive products alongside higher-priced menu items allows the chain to appeal to customers across income levels, Gordon said.

While Taco Bell remains important for growth, KFC has the opportunity to grow through restaurant openings. Yum reported overall 7% unit growth, with 878 KFC openings during the quarter. “The (Taco Bell) team is leaning in, continuing to play offense through the end of the year and into the beginning of 2027,” said CEO Chris Turner in yesterday’s earnings call.

KFC's international expansion is important as its U.S. business faces intense competition from chains such as Raising Cane's and Chick-fil-A. It has entered six new countries, Germany, Croatia, Ecuador, Moldova, Serbia and Sweden over the past year.

Still, the company's financial results require some context. Net income more than quadrupled to approximately $1.62 billion from $397 million a year earlier. However, that increase was largely driven by Yum's completed divestiture of Pizza Hut. Excluding Pizza Hut from both periods, Yum's core operating profit increased just 1% during the quarter.

Yum completed the sale of Pizza Hut's mainland China business to Yum China and its remaining global business to private equity firm LongRange Capital. The divestiture leaves the company focused on Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill, allowing management to concentrate resources on its remaining brands. The sale also raises questions about whether Yum will eventually seek another brand to diversify its portfolio.

“If growth starts slowing at KFC or Taco Bell internationally, that would really compel them,” said Ari Felhandler, a Morningstar analyst, on the possibility of an acquisition. “Although valuations have been hit a bit. It is a challenging time for the restaurant industry.”

posts.title: KFC shifts focus away from family-sized buckets to bring back customers
posts.author: irene-adeline-milanez
posts.excerpt: KFC has never struck Simone Gandy, 23, as a place that caters to someone her age. She associated the chain with feeding families with its buckets of chicken. “I don't know anyone who's diehard for KFC. I feel like it's meant to be a family meal place because of the whole bucket of chicken thing,”…
posts.content:
KFC has never struck Simone Gandy, 23, as a place that caters to someone her age. She associated the chain with feeding families with its buckets of chicken.

“I don't know anyone who's diehard for KFC. I feel like it's meant to be a family meal place because of the whole bucket of chicken thing,” she said. “I don't have a whole family to feed.”

Gandy recently visited the KFC two minutes from her home in Rosemont, Calif., partly to take advantage of the coupons she kept receiving in the mail. The nursing assistant ordered the five-piece Big Tenders Box with potato wedges and mashed potatoes to share with her girlfriend. She also ordered the Sweet Lightning drink, a peach-flavored, dirty soda, for a total of $21.

“We were debating if we went to Canes and got something of a similar size, it would probably be around 14 bucks,” Gandy said. “So this was more expensive.”

KFC has struggled to keep pace with fast-growing fried chicken competitors, such as Louisiana-based Raising Cane's and Georgia-based Chick-fil-A, in the U.S. Yum! Brands, KFC’s parent company, is betting on a revamped menu to revive its performance. This summer, Yum announced a plan to refresh KFC’s menu around boneless chicken, beverages and sauces in its top 20 markets by the end of 2027.

It won’t be easy. Yum is attempting to turn around its KFC business amid a challenging macroeconomic environment, as cautious consumer spending weighs on the fast-food industry. Fast-food companies have underperformed the broader market this year as many lower- and middle-income households face rising costs for food, gasoline and other everyday necessities.

The company does have wiggle room with Pizza Hut off its portfolio. Its sale to LongRange Capital and Yum China Holdings Inc in September for roughly $2.7 billion grants Yum the ability to shift its focus on improving KFC, along with Taco Bell.

“The chicken business has become brutally competitive, and the Raising Cane’s and Chick-fil-A's of the world have jumped on the bandwagon, mostly with chicken tenders,” said Stephen Zagor, restaurant consultant and Columbia University professor.

While KFC built its reputation as a family meal bucket destination for nearly a century, consumer sentiment has shifted towards dining out less, protein snacks and smaller portions, Zagor said.

In June, KFC introduced improved chicken tenders with over 20 sauces; “dunked” tenders, wings and sandwiches drenched in sauce; and a drink platform Kwench with boba, shakes, sparkling lemonades and iced coffees that the company said addresses “increasing demand for unique crafted beverages.”

“The KFC U.S. team is advancing its turnaround strategy, and KFC U.S. saw a strong consumer response to the launch of Popcorn Chicken in the third quarter, with the menu item selling out in many restaurants,” said CEO Chris Turner in November’s earnings call.

Yum did not respond to a request for comment on their current strategy.

Before the U.S., the U.K served as the testing grounds for KFC’s menu changes, Turner said during Yum’s July earnings call. It was part of a move by the company to invest nearly $2 billion dollars in KFC’s locations, supply chains and its workforce, according to the KFC U.K and Ireland 60th Anniversary report.

“Beverages have been super important in the restaurant industry,” said Ari Felhandler, Morningstar equity analyst. “When traffic's hard to come by, you want to raise whatever you can get out of a consumer.”

If KFC's turnaround strategy fails to gain traction, Yum could face pressure to find new sources of growth. With a one less brand in the company’s portfolio, the company has fewer businesses to offset continued weakness at KFC.

Same-store sales, which measures revenue generated by existing locations, were largely unchanged from a year earlier across its global portfolio, excluding Pizza Hut. Taco Bell saw a 4% decline, largely due to the cyclosplora outbreak discouraging traffic, while KFC recorded a modest 1% increase.

Analysts expect Yum to end this year with revenue of $8.66 billion, compared with $8.21 billion the previous year, and profits of $1.76 billion, a 3.4% increase. This growth is driven primarily by success overseas, where KFC faces lower regional competition in the fried chicken market.

With beef prices remaining high and consumers watching their spending, doubling down on chicken could be a helpful move for Yum. But the U.S. chicken market is crowded, with competitors like Wingstop, Raising Cane’s and Chick-fil-A giving customers plenty of options. Americans have become spoiled for choice when it comes to chicken, making it harder for KFC to stand out. To stay competitive, the chain is putting more focus on new sauces and flavors, such as garlic parmesan, pickle ranch and hot honey habanero.

“Customization gives you the ability to take a standardized product and customize it to something that you might find a little more appealing to you,” Zagor said.

While fast food companies have underperformed the broader market this year, Restaurant Brands International, which owns Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes and Firehouse Subs, has been a star amid the fast-food slump. It has seen its stock rise 7% since last year thanks to leadership change and aggressive brand reinvestment that directly translated into consistent sales growth, said John Gordon, Pacific Management Consulting Group analyst.

To drive KFC’s growth, Yum expanded the chain into new markets. Yum reported 7% overall unit growth, with 878 KFC openings in its most recent quarter. Over the past year, KFC has entered six countries, Germany, Croatia, Ecuador, Moldova, Serbia and Sweden. KFC plans to expand its Kwench rollout to 2000 restaurants by the end of 2026, double the amount of current participating restaurants.

KFC’s expansion ambitions may create logistical complexities as the company broadens its menu and market reach.

“Executing any concept with chicken is always challenging. You're ripping apart birds and breading them.” said Greg Francfort, Guggenheim equity analyst. “It's a complicated, labor-intensive and operationally challenging segment of the restaurant industry.”

posts.title: Uber’s Reckons with Driver Shortage In Latest Earnings
posts.author: sophiehayssen-2-2-2
posts.excerpt: Despite reporting third-quarter financial results that exceeded Wall Street's expectations, Uber revealed problems with attracting more drivers abroad amid high gas prices and increased competition. On Wednesday, Uber reported a revenue of $14.8 billion, a 10% increase year over year that beat analysts’ $14.67 billion estimate. Its net income was $512 million with earnings per…
posts.content:
Despite reporting third-quarter financial results that exceeded Wall Street's expectations, Uber revealed problems with attracting more drivers abroad amid high gas prices and increased competition.

On Wednesday, Uber reported a revenue of $14.8 billion, a 10% increase year over year that beat analysts’ $14.67 billion estimate. Its net income was $512 million with earnings per share of 25 cents, falling below analysts’ expectations of nine cents. Uber’s net income and earnings per share had a 92% decrease from last year, due to the release of deferred tax benefits. Gross bookings grew 20% to $59.8 billion, with similar 18%-22% growth expected for next quarter.

However, questions linger about rideshare, Uber’s hallmark service. This quarter, the division took a tumble for Uber. Rideshare’s growth in both revenue and gross bookings slowed over the past several quarters relative to delivery and shipping. This quarter, the headwinds came from abroad, notably Brazil and India, due to increased competition from other delivery businesses as well as high gas prices from the Iran war.

“I view the driver shortage as a meaningful but manageable near-term challenge,” said Ivan Feinseth, chief investment officer and director of research at Tigress Financial Partners LLC. “The principal risk is that prolonged shortages could require higher incentives, increase fares, and constrain growth.”

With no immediate end in sight for the Iran War, uncertainty lingers over Uber’s business. The company also said it chose not to release extensive forward guidance because of uncertainties around legal settlements and the financial impacts of acquisitions.

Due to the ongoing war, Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a key channel for oil delivery. With less supply on the market, prices have skyrocketed.

As of Sept. 7, gas in Brazil cost on average $4.80 per gallon. In India, it was slightly lower at $4.30 per gallon. Those prices are not too far off from the $4.41 that gas costs per gallon in the US."However, those in India and Brazil earn much lower salaries than those in the US, making those gas prices more of a burden." Americans enjoy an average yearly salary of $70,000, in India, the average monthly salary is the equivalent of $341. For Brazilians, it’s $686.

“It doesn't make as much sense for drivers to show up if the gas is costing more,” said Martin Szumski, equity research analyst at Morningstar.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi categorized the problem as a longer-term issue exacerbated by seasonal high demand. Khosrowshahi emphasized that while driver supply continued to be a challenge, demand remained strong.

“This is a good problem,” he said. “At the scale that we are operating at we still are running into supply constraints rather than demand constraints.”

Brazil is a major market for Uber with around 2% of its workforce driving full-time for delivery apps. This means there’s also lots of competition for drivers, which Khosrowshahi said caused driver supply issues last quarter. On Wednesday's call, Khosrowshahi noted that Uber would make strategic investments in driver retention and that much of Uber’s business, particularly in Brazil, depends on mopeds and e-bikes. He added that’s “one of the examples of supply that we need to add.”

Wall Street seemed to shrug off the stumble. On the day its earnings came out, Uber’s stock rose 6% from $68.28 to a high of $72.50.
